chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Yusuf ibn al-Sukht, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sulayman, from al-Fadl ibn Sulayman, from al-Abbas ibn Isa, who said:

Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) was straitened by financial difficulty, so he went to one of his freedmen and said to him, 'Lend me ten thousand dirhams until I have ease.' He said, 'No, because I do not have it, but I want a bond.' He said, 'So he tore a tassel from his robe and said to him, 'This is the bond.'

He said, 'So his freedman disliked that, so he was angered and said, 'Am I more worthy of fulfillment than Hajib ibn Zurara?' He said, 'You are more worthy of that than he is.' He said, 'So how did Hajib mortgage a bow, and it is merely a stick, for a hundred carriers, and he is an Infidel, yet he fulfills his pledge, while I would not fulfill my pledge for a tassel of my robe?'

He said, 'So the man took it from him and gave him the dirhams, and placed the tassel in a container. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, eased the wealth for him, so he carried it to the man, then said to him, 'I have brought your wealth, so give me my bond.' He said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! I lost it.' He said, 'Then do not take your wealth from me. One like me is not one who treats his pledge lightly.'
He said, 'So the man brought out the container, and there was the tassel in it. So Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) gave him the dirhams and took the tassel, threw it away, and departed.'

key_terms.حَاجِبُ بْنُ زُرَارَة: Hajib ibn Zurara, a companion of the Imams

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn and the tassel from his robe as a bond?
ai.summary: This narrative from al-Kafi highlights the meticulous adherence to contractual integrity by Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin), illustrating that the sanctity of a pledge lies in the sincerity of the promise rather than the material value of the collateral. By insisting on retrieving the simple tassel even after the debt was settled, he refutes the notion that minor obligations can be disregarded, a key principle in Shia jurisprudence regarding *amanah* (trusts). The incident serves as a practical lesson in personal accountability, emphasizing that one’s word is a binding covenant before God.

en.sarwar: 6. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Yusuf ibn al-Sukht from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sulayman from al-Fadl ibn Sulayman from al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Isa who has said the following:

“Once, Ali ibn Al-Husayn, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, was placed under pressure. He went to one of his Mawla’ (friend or follower) and asked him to lend him ten thousand dirham up to the time he is able to pay back. He (his friend) said, ‘No, because it is not with me; however, I want a promissory note.’ He (the narrator) has said, ‘He (the Imam) tore a piece from his gown and said this is the promissory note.’

His Mawla’ did not like it and became angry. He (the Imam) said, ‘Am I more trustworthy or Hajib ibn Zurarah?’ He (his Mawla’) replied, ‘You are more trustworthy than Hajib ibn Zurarah.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘How is it that Hajib by depositing his bow, only a piece of wood, as a guarantee to bail out one hundred, also being a non-Muslim, kept up to his words and I will not keep up my word despite depositing a piece of my gown?

5 He (the narrator) said that his Mawla’ took the piece of his gown and lent him the dirhams and placed the piece of fabric in a container. Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, granted him ease and he (the Imam) took the dirhams to return to the man and said, ‘Here is the dirhams. Where is the promissory note (the piece of my gown)? He replied, ‘I pray to Allah to keep my soul in service for your cause, I have lost it.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘You then cannot have your dirhams from me. One like me is not treated lightly in matters of trust.’

He (the narrator) has said, ‘He then brought the container and the piece of fabric was in it. Ali ibn Al-Husayn, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, gave the dirhams to him and took the piece of fabric and threw it away and left.’”
